meta.language: Arabic with transliteration and English meaning
meta.disclaimer: This is a study aid following the Hanafi school. It is not a substitute for a teacher. Where the schools differ, the difference is named rather than hidden. Anything marked with a note should be learned from a person, not a screen.
meta.translationNote: English meanings here are plain-language renderings written for this project, not a published translation.

qiyam.name: Qiyām
qiyam.body: Upright, eyes toward the place of prostration. Hanafi: a man folds his right hand over his left below the navel; a woman folds hers on the chest.
qiyam.why: The posture of attention and address. It is where the Qurʾān is recited, and the longest part of the prayer.

ruku.name: Rukūʿ
ruku.body: Bend forward with a flat back, hands gripping the knees, fingers spread. The back and neck level enough that water would not run off.
ruku.why: Bowing to a person was court protocol in the Persian and Byzantine world this emerged in. Reserving it for God alone was a political act, not only a devotional one.

qawmah.name: Qawmah
qawmah.body: Rise from the bow and stand fully upright before going down. Hanafis do not raise the hands here.
qawmah.why: A required pause, not a transition to rush. Early guidance criticised prayer performed so fast the body never settled.

sujud.name: Sujūd
sujud.body: Forehead, nose, both palms, both knees and the toes of both feet on the ground. Hanafi order going down: knees, then hands, then nose, then forehead.
sujud.why: The lowest posture a body can take, given to God alone. In a status-ordered society, putting the face on the floor was the strongest statement available.

jalsa.name: Jalsah
jalsa.body: Sit on the left foot with the right foot upright. Settle before going down again.
jalsa.why: The two prostrations are separate acts, not one long one.

qadah.name: Qaʿdah
qadah.body: Hanafi men sit the same way in both sittings — on the left foot, right foot upright. Hanafis do not use tawarruk. Women sit with both feet to the right.
qadah.why: The audience portion: having bowed and prostrated, you now sit and speak.

taslim.name: Taslīm
taslim.body: Turn the head right, then left, giving the greeting each time.
taslim.why: The prayer closes by turning back outward to the people beside you.

takbir.where: Said at the very start and again at every change of posture. At the start, men raise the hands to the ear lobes, women to the shoulders, then fold them.
takbir.then: It is akbar, greater, not kabīr, great — a comparative deliberately left unfinished. Greater than what? In a world of tribal gods, ancestral honour, clan chiefs and two rival empires, the open comparison swallowed all of them at once.
takbir.now: The first one is takbīrat al-iḥrām, the takbīr of restriction: once said, eating, speaking and walking away are off-limits until the prayer ends. Everything before it was your day.
takbir.varies: Hanafi men raise the hands to the ear lobes and fold below the navel. Shāfiʿīs raise to the shoulders and fold above the navel.

thana.arabic: سُبْحَانَكَ اللَّهُمَّ وَبِحَمْدِكَ، وَتَبَارَكَ اسْمُكَ، وَتَعَالَىٰ جَدُّكَ، وَلَا إِلَٰهَ غَيْرُكَ
thana.transliteration: Subḥānaka-llāhumma wa bi-ḥamdika, wa tabāraka-smuka, wa taʿālā jadduka, wa lā ilāha ghayruk
thana.meaning: Glory to You, O God, and praise. Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You.
thana.where: Standing, silently, straight after the opening takbīr — first unit only.

wordByWord.gloss: and there is no god but You

thana.then: Jadd in older Arabic meant standing, fortune, the grandeur attached to a lineage — exactly what a tribal society tracked most closely. The line assigns it to God.
thana.now: A warm-up before the Qurʾān: praise before request. Called the thanāʾ in Hanafi usage.
thana.varies: Hanafi and Ḥanbalī wording. Shāfiʿīs commonly open with wajjahtu wajhiya instead.

taawwudh.meaning: I take refuge with God from Satan, the rejected.
taawwudh.where: Standing, silently, after the thanāʾ — first unit only.
taawwudh.then: Rajīm comes from stoning — being pelted and driven out of the camp. The image is expulsion from the community, not merely dislike.
taawwudh.now: Said before reciting the Qurʾān generally, not only in prayer.

basmalah.meaning: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
basmalah.where: Standing, silently, immediately before al-Fātiḥa in every unit — silently even in the prayers recited aloud.
basmalah.then: Both names share the root r-ḥ-m, which also gives raḥim, the womb. Commentators drew the link deliberately: mercy that sustains something helpless without being asked.
basmalah.now: Opens 113 of the Qurʾān's 114 chapters, and is said before ordinary actions too.
basmalah.varies: Hanafis recite it silently always and do not count it as a verse of al-Fātiḥa for recitation. Shāfiʿīs count it as verse one and recite it aloud in the loud prayers.

fatiha_1.meaning: All praise belongs to God, Lord of all the worlds.
fatiha_1.where: Standing — al-Fātiḥa, verse 1 of 7. Recited in every unit of every prayer.

wordByWord.gloss: praise given because something deserves it

fatiha_1.then: ʿĀlamīn is plural — worlds, not world. Early commentators read it as every category of created thing. The opening claim is deliberately not local.
fatiha_1.now: The sentence has no verb and nobody doing the praising. It states a fact rather than making a promise, which is why it reads the same whoever says it.

fatiha_2.meaning: The Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
fatiha_2.where: Standing — al-Fātiḥa, verse 2 of 7. Recited in every unit of every prayer.
fatiha_2.then: Ar-Raḥmān was contested at the time — some Meccans objected to it as a name they did not recognise.
fatiha_2.now: Authority declared in the previous verse, then immediately qualified by mercy.

fatiha_3.meaning: Master of the Day of Judgement.
fatiha_3.where: Standing — al-Fātiḥa, verse 3 of 7. Recited in every unit of every prayer.
fatiha_3.then: Dīn here means reckoning or requital, not religion — it carries the sense of a debt settled. In a society run on obligation and blood-debt that was concrete language.
fatiha_3.now: Three verses moving outward then forward: praise, mercy, then time.

fatiha_4.meaning: You alone we serve, and You alone we ask for help.
fatiha_4.where: Standing — al-Fātiḥa, verse 4 of 7. Recited in every unit of every prayer.
fatiha_4.then: The word order carries the meaning. Ordinary Arabic would be naʿbuduka. Putting the object first makes it exclusive. The verse also switches from speaking about God to speaking to Him.
fatiha_4.now: The hinge of the surah — praise before it, request after. And it is plural: we, even alone in a room.

fatiha_5.meaning: Guide us along the straight path.
fatiha_5.where: Standing — al-Fātiḥa, verse 5 of 7. Recited in every unit of every prayer.
fatiha_5.then: Ṣirāṭ is a loanword, from Latin strata by way of Aramaic — a paved Roman road, not a desert track.
fatiha_5.now: The one request the whole surah is built to arrive at. Not wealth, not safety — direction.

fatiha_6.meaning: The path of those You have favoured.
fatiha_6.where: Standing — al-Fātiḥa, verse 6 of 7. Recited in every unit of every prayer.
fatiha_6.then: The path is defined by the people who walked it, not by a rule list.
fatiha_6.now: Read as a request to be placed in a lineage rather than handed instructions.

fatiha_7.meaning: Not those who earned anger, nor those who went astray.
fatiha_7.where: Standing — al-Fātiḥa, verse 7 of 7. Recited in every unit of every prayer.
fatiha_7.then: Two distinct failures: knowing the way and refusing it, and losing the way. The grammar keeps the anger passive rather than naming who was angry.
fatiha_7.now: The surah ends by marking the edges of the path; āmīn follows as the response.

ameen.where: Quietly at the end of al-Fātiḥa — silently in the Hanafi school, even in the loud prayers.

wordByWord.gloss: affirm it, let it be so

ameen.then: An old Semitic word shared with Hebrew and Aramaic, from a root meaning firm or reliable — the same root behind īmān, faith. It is not part of the surah.
ameen.now: Al-Fātiḥa's second half is a request, so āmīn is the amen at the end of the asking.
ameen.varies: Shāfiʿīs and Ḥanbalīs say it aloud in the loud prayers. Hanafis say it silently.

surah_slot.meaning: A further passage of the Qurʾān
surah_slot.where: Standing, after al-Fātiḥa — in the first two units only. At least three short verses or one long one.
surah_slot.now: Pick from the short surahs in this room, or any passage you have memorised.
surah_slot.varies: Hanafis treat this additional recitation as wājib in the first two units; other schools generally class it as sunnah.
surah_slot.note: placeholder — the room offers a surah picker here

ruku.meaning: Glory to my Lord, the Magnificent.
ruku.where: Bowing, back flat, hands gripping the knees with fingers spread. Said three times, quietly.

wordByWord.gloss: glory; declaring God free of any defect

ruku.then: Rabb did not mean a distant deity. It meant the one who owns, feeds and raises — used of a household master or the owner of livestock. It names daily dependence.
ruku.now: The name chosen is the immense, said in the posture where you have made yourself smaller. Body and sentence make the same claim.
ruku.varies: Three is the agreed minimum; five or seven are recommended when praying alone.

sami.meaning: God hears the one who praises Him.
sami.where: Said while straightening up from the bow. Praying alone or leading, say this and then the response. Behind an imam, say only the response.
sami.then: It is past tense — heard, not hears. Classical readings take this as settled fact rather than hope.
sami.now: One of the few points where imam and congregation say different things at once.

rabbana.meaning: Our Lord, to You belongs all praise.
rabbana.where: Said standing fully upright, answering samiʿa-llāhu li-man ḥamidah. Hanafis do not raise the hands here.
rabbana.then: Ḥamd is praise given because something deserves it, distinct from shukr, thanks for something received.
rabbana.varies: Shāfiʿīs and Ḥanbalīs raise the hands rising from rukūʿ; Hanafis raise them only at the opening takbīr. It is the clearest visual difference between the schools.

sujud.meaning: Glory to my Lord, the Most High.
sujud.where: In prostration — forehead, nose, both palms, both knees and the toes on the ground. Said three times, quietly. Hanafi order going down: knees, hands, nose, forehead.
sujud.then: Deliberately paired with the bowing phrase: the Magnificent when bent, the Most High when lowest to the ground.
sujud.now: Widely described as the closest point of the prayer — the lowest posture with the highest name.
sujud.varies: The nose touching alongside the forehead is required in the Hanafi school.

jalsa.meaning: My Lord, forgive me and have mercy on me.
jalsa.where: Sitting briefly between the two prostrations, on the left foot with the right foot upright.
jalsa.then: Ghafara means to cover or conceal — the same root behind the word for a helmet. Forgiveness as covering, not pretending it never happened.
jalsa.now: The only request inside the physical cycle; everything else in it is praise.
jalsa.varies: Hanafis treat the sitting as required but this supplication as recommended rather than obligatory.

tashahhud_1.meaning: All greetings belong to God, and all prayers, and all good things.
tashahhud_1.where: Sitting for the tashahhud — after the second unit, and again in the final sitting. Hanafi men sit on the left foot with the right foot upright in both sittings.
tashahhud_1.then: Taḥiyyāt was court vocabulary — the formal salutations and tributes offered to a king when you came before him. The line takes that whole register of tribute and redirects it.
tashahhud_1.now: Taught as an audience in three turns: greeting God, greeting the Prophet, greeting the righteous — then the declaration of faith.
tashahhud_1.varies: Hanafi and Ḥanbalī use Ibn Masʿūd's narration; Shāfiʿī uses Ibn ʿAbbās's; Mālikī uses ʿUmar's. This is the biggest wording fork in the prayer.

tashahhud_2.arabic: السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكَ أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ وَرَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ وَبَرَكَاتُهُ
tashahhud_2.transliteration: As-salāmu ʿalayka ayyuha-n-Nabiyyu wa raḥmatu-llāhi wa barakātuh
tashahhud_2.meaning: Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of God and His blessings.
tashahhud_2.where: Sitting for the tashahhud — after the second unit, and again in the final sitting. Hanafi men sit on the left foot with the right foot upright in both sittings.
tashahhud_2.then: The direct address was noticed early: the phrasing speaks to the Prophet rather than about him, and was kept unchanged after his death.
tashahhud_2.now: Hanafi manuals teach reciting the wording as narrated.
tashahhud_2.varies: Hanafi and Ḥanbalī use Ibn Masʿūd's narration; Shāfiʿī uses Ibn ʿAbbās's; Mālikī uses ʿUmar's. This is the biggest wording fork in the prayer.

tashahhud_3.arabic: السَّلَامُ عَلَيْنَا وَعَلَىٰ عِبَادِ اللَّهِ الصَّالِحِينَ
tashahhud_3.meaning: Peace be upon us, and upon the righteous servants of God.
tashahhud_3.where: Sitting for the tashahhud — after the second unit, and again in the final sitting. Hanafi men sit on the left foot with the right foot upright in both sittings.
tashahhud_3.then: Deliberately unbounded — no tribe, no era, no named group.
tashahhud_3.now: The widest greeting in the prayer, and it includes the person saying it.
tashahhud_3.varies: Hanafi and Ḥanbalī use Ibn Masʿūd's narration; Shāfiʿī uses Ibn ʿAbbās's; Mālikī uses ʿUmar's. This is the biggest wording fork in the prayer.

tashahhud_4.arabic: أَشْهَدُ أَن لَّا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا عَبْدُهُ وَرَسُولُهُ
tashahhud_4.transliteration: Ash-hadu an lā ilāha illa-llāhu wa ash-hadu anna Muḥammadan ʿabduhu wa rasūluh
tashahhud_4.meaning: I bear witness that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger.
tashahhud_4.where: Sitting for the tashahhud — after the second unit, and again in the final sitting. Hanafi men sit on the left foot with the right foot upright in both sittings.

wordByWord.gloss: I bear witness — legal testimony, not opinion

tashahhud_4.then: Ash-hadu is courtroom language, the verb for testifying before a judge. And servant comes before messenger, guarding against elevating the Prophet beyond a human being.
tashahhud_4.now: In the Hanafi school the right index finger is raised at lā ilāha and lowered at illa-llāh — the gesture tracking the sentence.
tashahhud_4.varies: Hanafi and Ḥanbalī use Ibn Masʿūd's narration; Shāfiʿī uses Ibn ʿAbbās's; Mālikī uses ʿUmar's. This is the biggest wording fork in the prayer.

salawat_1.arabic: اللَّهُمَّ صَلِّ عَلَىٰ مُحَمَّدٍ وَعَلَىٰ آلِ مُحَمَّدٍ، كَمَا صَلَّيْتَ عَلَىٰ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَعَلَىٰ آلِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ، إِنَّكَ حَمِيدٌ مَجِيدٌ
salawat_1.transliteration: Allāhumma ṣalli ʿalā Muḥammadin wa ʿalā āli Muḥammad, kamā ṣallayta ʿalā Ibrāhīma wa ʿalā āli Ibrāhīm, innaka Ḥamīdun Majīd
salawat_1.meaning: O God, send blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Abraham and the family of Abraham. You are Praiseworthy, Glorious.
salawat_1.where: Final sitting only, immediately after the tashahhud.
salawat_1.then: The comparison to Abraham matters: Arabs traced descent to him through Ishmael, so the link placed the new community inside an existing story rather than starting a new one.
salawat_1.now: Followed immediately by the same paragraph with bārik in place of ṣalli.

salawat_2.arabic: اللَّهُمَّ بَارِكْ عَلَىٰ مُحَمَّدٍ وَعَلَىٰ آلِ مُحَمَّدٍ، كَمَا بَارَكْتَ عَلَىٰ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَعَلَىٰ آلِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ، إِنَّكَ حَمِيدٌ مَجِيدٌ
salawat_2.transliteration: Allāhumma bārik ʿalā Muḥammadin wa ʿalā āli Muḥammad, kamā bārakta ʿalā Ibrāhīma wa ʿalā āli Ibrāhīm, innaka Ḥamīdun Majīd
salawat_2.meaning: O God, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Abraham and the family of Abraham. You are Praiseworthy, Glorious.
salawat_2.where: Final sitting, straight after the paragraph above.

wordByWord.gloss: bless — from barakah, increase that keeps giving

salawat_2.then: Barakah is not blessing in the abstract. It means something that yields beyond what it should — a well that does not run dry.
salawat_2.now: Learned as one block with the first paragraph; it is mostly the same sentence with one word changed.

dua_final.arabic: رَبَّنَا آتِنَا فِي الدُّنْيَا حَسَنَةً وَفِي الْآخِرَةِ حَسَنَةً وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ
dua_final.transliteration: Rabbanā ātinā fi-d-dunyā ḥasanatan wa fi-l-ākhirati ḥasanatan wa qinā ʿadhāba-n-nār
dua_final.meaning: Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the next, and protect us from the fire.
dua_final.where: Final sitting, after the ṣalawāt and before the salām. Recommended, not obligatory.

wordByWord.gloss: this world — literally the nearer one
the next — literally the later one

dua_final.then: Dunyā and ākhirah are a matched pair — the nearer and the later — so the verse asks for both halves of existence without treating either as disposable.
dua_final.now: Probably the most widely recited supplication among Muslims.
dua_final.varies: Any lawful supplication is permitted here.

taslim_r.meaning: Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God.
taslim_r.where: Turn the head fully to the right — far enough that the cheek is visible from behind — and say it.
taslim_r.then: Salām shares a root with wholeness and with islām. As a greeting it was a guarantee of safety: you are safe from me.
taslim_r.now: The prayer opens by leaving the world and closes by turning back to it.

taslim_l.meaning: Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God.
taslim_l.where: Turn the head fully to the left and say it again. The prayer is now finished.
taslim_l.then: Traditionally understood as greeting those beside you and the angels recording on each side.
taslim_l.now: This closes the state the opening takbīr began.

qunut.arabic: اللَّهُمَّ إِنَّا نَسْتَعِينُكَ وَنَسْتَغْفِرُكَ وَنُؤْمِنُ بِكَ وَنَتَوَكَّلُ عَلَيْكَ وَنُثْنِي عَلَيْكَ الْخَيْرَ وَنَشْكُرُكَ وَلَا نَكْفُرُكَ وَنَخْلَعُ وَنَتْرُكُ مَنْ يَفْجُرُكَ. اللَّهُمَّ إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَلَكَ نُصَلِّي وَنَسْجُدُ وَإِلَيْكَ نَسْعَىٰ وَنَحْفِدُ نَرْجُو رَحْمَتَكَ وَنَخْشَىٰ عَذَابَكَ إِنَّ عَذَابَكَ بِالْكُفَّارِ مُلْحِقٌ
qunut.transliteration: Allāhumma innā nastaʿīnuka wa nastaghfiruka wa nuʾminu bika wa natawakkalu ʿalayka wa nuthnī ʿalayka-l-khayra wa nashkuruka wa lā nakfuruka wa nakhlaʿu wa natruku man yafjuruk. Allāhumma iyyāka naʿbudu wa laka nuṣallī wa nasjudu wa ilayka nasʿā wa naḥfidu narjū raḥmataka wa nakhshā ʿadhābaka inna ʿadhābaka bi-l-kuffāri mulḥiq
qunut.meaning: O God, we seek Your help and Your forgiveness, we believe in You and rely on You, we praise You for all good and thank You and are not ungrateful, and we cast off and leave whoever disobeys You. O God, You alone we worship, to You we pray and prostrate, to You we strive and hasten. We hope for Your mercy and fear Your punishment — Your punishment surely overtakes those who reject.
qunut.where: Standing in the third unit of witr, after the recitation. Say Allāhu akbar raising the hands, then fold them and recite this quietly, then bow.

wordByWord.gloss: we cast off — literally we take off, as with a garment

qunut.then: Qunūt originally meant standing in sustained, obedient devotion. Nakhlaʿu is the verb for removing a garment or shedding a skin — the image is of stepping out of an allegiance rather than merely disagreeing with it.
qunut.now: A Hanafi marker: because witr is wājib in this school, the qunūt inside it comes up every night.
qunut.varies: Shāfiʿīs recite a qunūt in Fajr instead, aloud, with different wording. Hanafis do not recite qunūt in Fajr except in times of public calamity.
qunut.note: Check this wording against your own teacher or a Hanafi manual before relying on it. Minor variations in the closing phrase exist between printed versions.

ayat_kursi.arabic: اللَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ ۚ لَا تَأْخُذُهُ سِنَةٌ وَلَا نَوْمٌ ۚ لَهُ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ ۗ مَن ذَا الَّذِي يَشْفَعُ عِندَهُ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِهِ ۚ يَعْلَمُ مَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَمَا خَلْفَهُمْ ۖ وَلَا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَيْءٍ مِّنْ عِلْمِهِ إِلَّا بِمَا شَاءَ ۚ وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ ۖ وَلَا يَئُودُهُ حِفْظُهُمَا ۚ وَهُوَ الْعَلِيُّ الْعَظِيمُ
ayat_kursi.transliteration: Allāhu lā ilāha illā huwa-l-Ḥayyu-l-Qayyūm. Lā taʾkhudhuhu sinatun wa lā nawm. Lahu mā fi-s-samāwāti wa mā fi-l-arḍ. Man dha-lladhī yashfaʿu ʿindahu illā bi-idhnih. Yaʿlamu mā bayna aydīhim wa mā khalfahum, wa lā yuḥīṭūna bi-shayʾin min ʿilmihi illā bimā shāʾ. Wasiʿa kursiyyuhu-s-samāwāti wa-l-arḍ, wa lā yaʾūduhu ḥifẓuhumā, wa huwa-l-ʿAliyyu-l-ʿAẓīm
ayat_kursi.meaning: God — there is no god but He, the Living, the Sustaining. Neither drowsiness nor sleep takes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Who could intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what lies before them and behind them, and they grasp nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. His seat extends over the heavens and the earth, and guarding them does not weary Him. He is the Most High, the Magnificent.
ayat_kursi.where: Recited after each obligatory prayer, after the tasbīḥ. Not part of the prayer itself.

wordByWord.gloss: the self-subsisting who sustains everything else
drowsiness — the state just before sleep

ayat_kursi.then: One long sentence, Sūrat al-Baqarah verse 255. Sinah and nawm are deliberately paired — not even the drowsiness that precedes sleep. Set against surrounding cultures whose gods slept, tired and needed feeding, the denial is pointed.
ayat_kursi.now: Widely memorised and recited at night and before travel as well as after prayer.
ayat_kursi.note: Long verse. Check it against a muṣḥaf before memorising from a screen.

fajr.name: Fajr
fajr.about: The day's first prayer, in the dark or half-light before the sun rises. Recited aloud.

sequence.cue: Stand and recite.
Say Allāhu akbar as you bow.
Stand fully upright. Do not rush this.

surahs.name: Al-Ikhlāṣ

verses.meaning: Say: He is God, One.
God, the Eternal Refuge.
He did not father, and was not fathered.

verses.transliteration: Wa lam yakun lahu kufuwan aḥad
verses.meaning: And there is nothing comparable to Him.

surahs.then: Four lines answering a direct question the Meccans put to the Prophet: describe your God's lineage. Every Arabian deity had a genealogy. The answer refuses the frame — no parent, no child, no equal.
surahs.now: Traditionally said to equal a third of the Qurʾān. Usually the first surah anyone learns.

surahs.name: Al-ʿAṣr

verses.meaning: By time.
Humankind is in loss.

verses.arabic: إِلَّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالْحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالصَّبْرِ
verses.transliteration: Illā-lladhīna āmanū wa ʿamilū-ṣ-ṣāliḥāti wa tawāṣaw bi-l-ḥaqqi wa tawāṣaw bi-ṣ-ṣabr
verses.meaning: Except those who believe, do right, and urge each other to truth and to patience.

surahs.then: Khusr is a merchant's word — loss on a transaction, capital gone. Addressed to a trading city, it frames a life as a deal running at a deficit unless four things are present.
surahs.now: Three verses, and two of the four conditions are about other people, not private belief.

surahs.name: Al-Kawthar

verses.meaning: We have given you abundance.
So pray to your Lord and offer sacrifice.
It is the one who hates you who is cut off.

surahs.then: The shortest chapter in the Qurʾān. Abtar meant a man with no surviving sons — whose line and name would end. Opponents used the word against the Prophet after his sons died. The surah turns it back.
surahs.now: Widely recited because it is three short verses; the background changes how the last line lands.

surahs.name: Al-Falaq

verses.meaning: Say: I take refuge with the Lord of daybreak,
from the harm of what He created,

verses.transliteration: Wa min sharri ghāsiqin idhā waqab
verses.meaning: from the harm of darkness as it settles,
from the harm of those who blow on knots,

verses.transliteration: Wa min sharri ḥāsidin idhā ḥasad
verses.meaning: and from the harm of the envier when he envies.

surahs.then: Al-Falaq and an-Nās are known together as the two chapters of refuge. Both name the protector first, then list what you are protected from.
surahs.now: Recited together very commonly, in prayer and outside it.

surahs.name: An-Nās

verses.meaning: Say: I take refuge with the Lord of people,
the King of people,
the God of people,
from the harm of the whisperer who withdraws,
who whispers in the chests of people,
from among jinn and people.

surahs.then: Three divine names stacked at the start — Lord, King, God — before the threat is named.
surahs.now: Closes the Qurʾān, paired with al-Falaq.

sunnahNote: In the Hanafi school a surah is recited after al-Fātiḥa in every unit of a sunnah or voluntary prayer, not only the first two — this is one of the clearest differences between a sunnah prayer and an obligatory one. A four-unit sunnah is prayed as one set of four with a sitting after the second unit.

differences.topic: Raising the hands during the prayer
differences.hanafi: Only at the opening takbīr, plus the witr qunūt and the Eid takbīrs.
differences.others: Shāfiʿī and Ḥanbalī also raise them going into and rising from the bow. The most visible difference if you pray beside someone from another school.

differences.topic: Where the hands are folded when standing
differences.hanafi: Men below the navel, women on the chest.
differences.others: Shāfiʿī: above the navel. Mālikī: commonly hanging at the sides.
Shāfiʿī and Ḥanbalī say it aloud in the loud prayers.

differences.hanafi: Silently in every unit; not counted as a verse of al-Fātiḥa for recitation.
differences.others: Shāfiʿī counts it as verse one and recites it aloud in the loud prayers.

differences.hanafi: You do not recite al-Fātiḥa — you listen.
differences.others: Shāfiʿī: the follower recites it. Ḥanbalī: during the silent pauses.
Shāfiʿī uses Ibn ʿAbbās's, Mālikī uses ʿUmar's, Ḥanbalī uses Ibn Masʿūd's like the Hanafis.

differences.hanafi: The same as the middle sitting — left foot under, right foot upright.
differences.others: Shāfiʿī and Ḥanbalī sit tawarruk, left foot out to the side.

differences.hanafi: Wājib, three units joined, with a qunūt in the third.
differences.others: Other schools treat it as a strong sunnah, often structured differently.
Shāfiʿī, Mālikī and Ḥanbalī use one. This is why prayer apps have a Hanafi setting.

differences.hanafi: One salām, then the two prostrations, then tashahhud and the full salām.
differences.others: Shāfiʿī places both prostrations before the salām.

differences.hanafi: Not recited, except in times of public calamity.
differences.others: Shāfiʿīs recite it in Fajr regularly, aloud, after rising from the bow in the second unit.
